title: Consider your ways (Haggai 1:2–8)
hook: you eat but aren't full; you earn wages into a bag with holes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zephaniah's surprise: he will sing over you. Your line was sung over. Did you tell someone, in words or a tune, that you're glad they exist? Day four hundred ninety-three.

Payday. The money lands in your account, and by the end of the week, somehow, it's gone. Not on anything big. Just leaking. Groceries that didn't last, subscriptions you forgot, little fixes on things that keep breaking. You work hard and never quite get ahead. Twenty-five centuries ago, a prophet named Haggai described exactly that feeling, and he did it with an image anyone who's ever carried coins can picture. A purse with a hole in the bottom. He wasn't talking to people who were lazy. He was talking to people who were busy, and tired, and couldn't figure out why it never felt like enough.
screen: `A PURSE WITH A HOLE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Haggai is one of the few prophets whose words come with exact dates. His first message is dated to a specific day in 520 BC. The exiles have come home from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the temple is still a ruin, years after their return. People are saying it isn't the right time to rebuild. Haggai's answer, in the King James Bible: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" Cieled means paneled, finished nicely, while God's house sits in rubble. Then comes the line that becomes today's carry: "Consider your ways." In Hebrew it's more vivid: set your heart on your ways. Look hard at where your life is going. And then the list: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes." Every line has the same shape. Effort in, nothing to show for it. Haggai's diagnosis is that the people have put their own houses first and left the center empty. So the cure is surprisingly practical: go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. Christians read Haggai in more than one way. Some hear it about church buildings and giving. Many hear it more broadly: when the most important thing in a life is left in ruins, everything else leaks. And here's the good news hiding in the book: the people actually listened. Within weeks, according to Haggai's own dates, they started rebuilding.
screen: `520 BC: THE TEMPLE STILL IN RUINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at where your effort leaks. Settle, and breathe. Picture your last week as a bag you've been filling. Your time, your energy, your money, your attention. Where are the holes? Maybe it's hours on a screen that left you emptier. Maybe it's worry about something you can't change. Maybe it's work that never touches what you care most about. Don't fix it now. Just find one hole. Then ask Haggai's question: what's the thing at the center that I've left in ruins? If you pray, you can set that before God and ask for one first step. If you don't, simply name it, and name the first piece of wood. The bell holds the time.
Consider your ways. Haggai's call to returned exiles who were busy and never satisfied: set your heart on where your life is going.
Your line: consider your ways. Today, patch one hole in the bag. Close one tab, cancel one thing, or give ten minutes to what matters most. Day four hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Christians often read Haggai when a church is building or rebuilding, and many use its call to consider your ways as a prompt for an honest review of how they spend their time and money.

original.note: Hebrew: way, road, path. Haggai asks the people to set their hearts on their ways.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stern line, like think about what you've done.
what it means: busy, tired people are asked to look at why their effort keeps leaking, and to rebuild what matters most.
what a scholar hears: in Hebrew it's set your heart on your ways, spoken in 520 BC to exiles who had come home to a temple in ruins.

sources.quoted: Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

notes: Haggai 1:1 is dated to the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year, generally 520 BC (late August). Confirm.
Haggai 1:15 dates the start of work to the 24th day of the same month: 'within weeks'. Confirm.
'Set your heart on your ways' as the literal Hebrew (simu levavchem al darcheichem). Confirm.
Two Christian readings (church buildings and giving; ordering life around what matters most) given without ranking.
